audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the Saelzer 1976:134 quotation is confirmed verbatim in the held PDF at the stated page. (2) The deciding citation is a 1976 SIL 'provisional phonology' article, but the standard reference grammar (Seki 2000, held) states the same rule in its stress section §22.3 p.419 — non-contrastive final stress on free forms of 2+ syllables, atonic prefixes/proclitics, a split between tonic (-ite) and atonic (-a) suffixes, alternating secondary stress leftward — and Silva 1981:73 (fetched sources now) independently confirms final stress on all free forms with atonic prefixes and some atonic suffixes (case -a). sources.quote: "2.1.4. Accentuation. Primary stress falls regularly on the last syllable of words. ... Secondary stress commonly occurs on alternating syllables counting backwards from the syllable of primary stress, in verbs without suffixes. When a noun is affixed, the primary stress may move to the last syllable of the new word or stay on the final syllable of the root. It will frequently fall in the place of the secondary stress."
